title: The training principles series: specificity
summary: He argues the strength-sport principle of specificity applies to bodybuilding too. Pick compound lifts that suit you, then surround them with close variations that carry over, because lifting is a neurological skill and constantly novel exercises keep you relearning and lower your tonnage. Odd exercises are fine as exceptions, never as the rule.
claims: Strength athletes stay within a range of specificity, using squat variations and accessories that build the main lift without repeating the exact pattern all the time

Variations within specificity reduce overuse injuries, prevent imbalances by training different angles, and help bypass the so-called law of accommodation, which volume and intensity manipulation can also bypass
Saying bodybuilders do not need specificity is condescending; bodybuilding is as intellectual and strategic as powerlifting
He chose compound lifts that agree with him first, then picked variations and accessories that complement them
You lift with your nervous system: practice builds neural pathways and proficiency, and stopping unlearns them; after a year off squats you feel wobbly, though you relearn faster than the first time
Shocking the muscle is counterproductive; rotating in unfamiliar lifts keeps lowering tonnage while you relearn and makes you a technician of new tricks rather than a master
If the squat is your main knee flexion, use front squats, box squats and SSB squats rather than leg press, single-leg squats and lunges
Never put a lift in your program that has no close neighbours; occasional odd exercises are fine as exceptions
When all your lower-body lifts are similar enough to feed into each other, you can push much more tonnage and progress better
Small modifications to a lift are enough to avoid overuse and accommodation; you do not need to jump from barbell to dumbbell bench
Exercises that are never replicated in the program progress slowly; keep them if you love them, but do not make the exception the rule
